clinicalPearls: Inflammation of the sacroiliac joint, a hallmark of axial spondyloarthritis but with several causes
Presents with inflammatory-type buttock or low back pain, often alternating, with morning stiffness
Common causes are the spondyloarthritides (ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic, reactive and enteropathic arthritis)
Infective (septic) sacroiliitis is an important distinct cause, usually unilateral with acute severe pain and systemic features
MRI detects active inflammation (bone marrow oedema) earlier than radiographic changes
Management depends on the cause: immunomodulation for inflammatory disease, antimicrobials for infection
reference.pathophysiology: Sacroiliitis is inflammation of the sacroiliac joint that may be immune-mediated or infective. In spondyloarthritis, enthesitis and synovial inflammation at the joint are driven by genetic susceptibility (HLA-B27) and dysregulated immunity, producing bone marrow oedema, erosion and, over time, ankylosis. Septic sacroiliitis results from haematogenous or contiguous infection of the joint. Mechanical and degenerative processes can also inflame the joint. The pattern (unilateral versus bilateral, acute versus chronic) and systemic features help distinguish the causes.
additionalDifferentials: Referred pain from the hip or lumbar spine
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the sacroiliac joints for active inflammation
Assessment for features of spondyloarthritis and its extra-articular manifestations
Blood cultures and joint sampling where infection is suspected
redFlags: Acute severe unilateral pain with fever suggesting septic sacroiliitis
Immunosuppression or injecting drug use raising infection risk
Neurological deficit suggesting an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the cause; inflammatory sacroiliitis is controllable with modern therapy though it may progress to ankylosis, and septic sacroiliitis does well with prompt antimicrobial treatment.
pitfalls: Missing septic sacroiliitis, which needs urgent antimicrobial therapy
Relying on radiographs and missing early inflammation seen on MRI
Attributing inflammatory back pain to mechanical causes
